# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Meta-analysts increasingly work with databases in which individual studies contribute more than one effect size. Estimates from the same study share samples, data, and researchers, so they are not independent. This is the norm rather than the exception. Reviewing 1,000 meta-analyses across ten disciplines, Wu, Duan, Reed, and Tipton (2026) find that 57 percent contained dependent effect sizes, yet fewer than half of these (47 percent) made any statistical adjustment for the dependence. Wu and Reed (2026) find the same pattern in 100 meta-analyses published in leading management and marketing journals: 78 percent acknowledge that their effect sizes are dependent, but only 37 percent of those use a multilevel or multivariate model capable of addressing it. Current practice has not caught up with the data.

Dependence arises in several ways. A study may report effects for several outcome measures, for several follow-up periods on the same sample, or for several treatment groups compared with a common control group. Studies by the same research team, or studies that use overlapping samples, can also be related. Ignoring this dependence has two costs. First, treating the estimates as independent overstates the amount of information in the database. Standard errors are then too small, and hypothesis tests and confidence intervals do not have their nominal properties. Second, an analysis that assumes independence discards information about how the estimates covary, so its estimates of moderator effects are less efficient than they could be.

Dependence is not the only problem. Most meta-analytic databases are also affected by publication bias: estimates that are statistically significant, or that have the expected sign, are more likely to be reported than others. Here too, practice lags behind recommendations. Wu and Reed (2026) find that, among meta-analyses that test for publication bias, fewer than half go on to report a bias-corrected estimate. Most rely instead on the funnel plot and Fail-safe N, which have limited power to detect bias and offer no way to correct for it. The two problems are linked. A correction for publication bias must allow for the dependence among estimates, and recent work has developed corrections that do so (Rodgers and Pustejovsky, 2021; Chen and Pustejovsky, 2026; Pustejovsky, Citkowicz, and Joshi, 2026; van Aert, Riley, and Jackson, 2026; Bartoš, Maier, and Wagenmakers, 2026). These corrections differ in what they assume about how selection operates. Some treat each estimate as selected on its own statistical significance; others treat the study as the unit of selection, so that whether a study is published depends on how many of its estimates are significant. They need not give the same answer.

This creates a practical problem for applied researchers. The methods are scattered across a methodological literature, several are computationally demanding, and it is not obvious how they fit together: which dependence model to use, which correction for publication bias, and in what order the analyses should be done. A protocol addresses this problem in two ways. First, it sets out a single sequence of decisions and supplies ready-to-run R code for each step, which lowers the cost of applying recommended methods. Second, it limits what Simmons, Nelson, and Simonsohn (2011) call researcher degrees of freedom. Data cleaning, model specification, and bias correction each involve many defensible choices. Taken together, these choices give the analyst considerable latitude over the final estimate, a hazard that Gelman and Loken (2014) describe as a "garden of forking paths." Committing in advance to a documented sequence of estimators, corrections, and decision rules makes it less likely that the results guide the choice of method. It also lets the reader check what was done.

This protocol combines two lines of methodological work. The first is robust variance estimation. Pustejovsky and Tipton (2022) show that the correlated and hierarchical effects (CHE) working model, which allows for between-study heterogeneity, within-study heterogeneity, and correlated sampling errors, is a realistic description of the dependence found in social science meta-analyses. Combined with small-sample cluster-robust standard errors (Tipton, 2015; Tipton and Pustejovsky, 2015), it supports valid inference even when the working model is only approximately correct. The second is Robust Bayesian Meta-Analysis (RoBMA; Maier, Bartoš, and Wagenmakers, 2023), which averages over competing models of the selection process rather than committing to one. Its multilevel and meta-regression extensions (Bartoš, Maier, and Wagenmakers, 2026; Bartoš, Maier, Stanley, and Wagenmakers, 2025) handle dependent effect sizes and moderators, and version 4.1 of the RoBMA package estimates it with the CHE working model.

After data cleaning (@sec-cleaning) and a preliminary analysis (@sec-prelim), the protocol proceeds in five steps. First, @sec-estimators presents five estimators of the mean effect, leading up to CHE as the preferred dependence model. Second, @sec-pubbias compares three corrections for publication bias, all embedded within a dependence context. PET-PEESE (Stanley and Doucouliagos, 2014) treats selection as a smooth relationship between effect size and its standard error. Step-function selection models (Pustejovsky, Citkowicz, and Joshi, 2026) model the selection process directly. RoBMA is a Bayesian method that averages over both kinds of model. Third, @sec-diagnosis uses diagnostics of how selection operates in the data to choose one correction as the primary approach. Fourth, @sec-metareg estimates meta-regressions for all three corrections and uses them to predict the effect for a study that follows best research practice. Finally, @sec-sensitivity reports the final estimates from the primary approach and checks whether the conclusions depend on that choice. @sec-conclusion concludes. [Appendix A](#sec-app-rho) reports how sensitive the results are to the assumed correlation between the sampling errors of estimates from the same study, and [Appendix B](#sec-app-outliers) examines outliers and influential studies.

## How to Use This Protocol {#sec-intro-use}

**A quick start.** You do not need to read the whole protocol before running it. Download the project folder from GitHub, install JAGS (see @sec-software), open `MA_Protocol.Rproj`, then open `Protocol_Combined.qmd` and choose Run > Run All (Ctrl+Alt+R). The example data and saved results for the slowest models are included, so a complete pass takes about 45 minutes and confirms that every step runs on your computer. The explanations can then be read section by section, as they become relevant to your own analysis.

The protocol comes in two forms. The source is a Quarto document, `Protocol_Combined.qmd`, which combines the explanation with the R code that produces each table and figure. Opened in RStudio, it lets a researcher run the analysis by clicking through the code chunks in order, using the "Run" arrow on each chunk. Rendering the .qmd produces `Protocol_Combined.html`, the self-contained document most readers will read. The HTML version cannot run the code, but it shows it. The code for each step is folded under a "Code" button, and the "Code" menu at the top of the page shows the full .qmd source. The .qmd file, the rendered HTML, the R scripts, and the data are available at [github.com/bobreednz/ma-protocol-dependent-effects](https://github.com/bobreednz/ma-protocol-dependent-effects). To apply the protocol to a new meta-analysis, a researcher substitutes their own dataset and adjusts the variable names in the scripts, rather than writing new code for each method.

The protocol is illustrated throughout with data from Xue, Reed, and van Aert (2025), a meta-analysis of the association between social capital and economic growth published in the *Journal of Economic Surveys*. The dataset contains 957 effect size estimates from 83 studies, expressed as Fisher's z-transformed partial correlation coefficients (PCCs). It serves only as a running example. Because the example comes from economics, so do its moderators, its best-practice choices, and benchmarks such as the Doucouliagos (2011) guidelines for interpreting partial correlations. The same steps apply to any database of dependent effect sizes, although some details depend on the effect size; @sec-robma, for example, explains how RoBMA handles effect sizes other than Fisher's z.

Each analytical section has the same structure. A short explanation says what is being estimated and why. A "Run the script" chunk sources the R script that does the work, and a "Display the output" chunk reads the script's saved output into the document. Two kinds of commentary follow the output. "What to look for" explains how to read the output, in terms that apply to any dataset. "In this example" reports what the output shows for the social capital data. Where the researcher must make a choice before going on, a "Decision point" sets out the options and how to choose among them.

## Software Setup {#sec-software}

All analyses are conducted in R. Rendering the protocol also requires Quarto, which is included with recent versions of RStudio. Before running any script, run `Protocol_Install.R`, shown below. It installs every R package the protocol needs and prints the versions installed. The RoBMA results reported in this protocol were produced with RoBMA 4.1.1 and BayesTools 0.4.0.

The `metaselection` package, used for the step-function selection models in Sections [-@sec-pubbias] and [-@sec-metareg], is now available from CRAN. The results reported in this protocol were produced with version 0.1.5, a development build installed from GitHub.

RoBMA also requires JAGS (Just Another Gibbs Sampler), a standalone program that performs the underlying MCMC sampling. JAGS is not an R package and cannot be installed with `install.packages()`. Download and install JAGS (version 4.3.1 or newer) from <https://mcmc-jags.sourceforge.io/> before running `Protocol_Install.R`.


### Reproducibility: project setup instead of `setwd()`

This protocol uses the `here` package (installed by `Protocol_Install.R`) together with an RStudio Project file, `MA_Protocol.Rproj`, which is included in the project folder alongside the scripts and data, so that no script or the protocol document itself needs a hardcoded path.

To work with this protocol on your own machine: (1) download or clone the entire project folder, keeping all scripts, data files, and `MA_Protocol.Rproj` together in one folder; (2) open the project by double-clicking `MA_Protocol.Rproj` (or, in RStudio, File > Open Project); this sets your working directory to the project root automatically, with no path to edit. Every script then locates its files with `here("filename")` rather than a bare `"filename"`, which resolves relative to the project root regardless of your operating system or username.

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(here)        # resolves file paths relative to the project root (.Rproj)
library(readxl)     # read_excel() used in all display chunks
```

# Data Cleaning and Quality Checks {#sec-cleaning}

Before any analysis can proceed, the raw dataset must be inspected and cleaned. This step is essential for any meta-analysis, but it requires particular care when effect sizes are dependent, because errors in coding, such as duplicated observations or inconsistent standard errors, can be difficult to detect when multiple estimates come from the same source.

## What the cleaning script does {#sec-cleaning-script}

The script `Protocol_DataCleaning.R` runs eight sequential quality checks on the raw dataset (`SCData (20240508).dta`). These checks address the most common data problems in meta-analytic databases:

1. **Missing values.** Identifies observations with missing values in any variable.
2. **Duplicates and coding conflicts.** Detects rows that are exact copies of one another (true duplicates) and rows from the same study that share the same effect size, standard error, and t-statistic but differ in their coding of other variables (coding conflicts).
3. **Valid ranges.** Verifies that binary variables contain only 0/1 values and that key continuous variables (standard errors, degrees of freedom, publication year) fall within plausible bounds.
4. **Mutual exclusivity.** Verifies that each set of mutually exclusive dummy variables (social capital type, outcome type, geographic level, region, endogeneity treatment) sums to exactly one for every observation.
5. **Internal consistency of derived variables.** Verifies that the Fisher's z, partial correlation, and t-statistic variables satisfy their defining relationships (z = atanh(pcc); t = pcc/se).
6. **Standard error consistency.** Flags observations whose reported standard error is smaller than the value implied by the reported degrees of freedom, distinguishing minor discrepancies (likely rounding artifacts) from major ones (possible coding errors).
7. **Outlier effect sizes.** Flags observations with exceptionally large effect sizes, using both an absolute threshold and a distance-from-the-mean criterion.
8. **Small degrees of freedom.** Flags observations from regressions with very few degrees of freedom, which may yield unreliable standard errors.

**A note on traceability to source studies.** None of the eight checks above can substitute for being able to trace a specific effect size back to its exact location in the original publication. The dataset used in this protocol (`SCData (20240508).dta`) does not include variables recording the table, page, and regression (or column) number in the source paper from which each estimate was extracted. This is a limitation of the illustrative dataset, not a feature of good practice: whenever a flagged or otherwise suspect observation needs to be checked, the researcher must be able to open the original paper and locate the exact estimate in question, which is only possible if this information was recorded at the time of data extraction. We recommend that any meta-analytic dataset include these identifiers as standard practice, alongside the study identifier (`newid`) already present here.

No observations are dropped during this step. Instead, the observation-level checks add binary flag variables to the dataset, and an omnibus flag (`flag_any`) marks any observation that triggers at least one of them. It is up to the researcher to inspect these flags and decide which, if any, to act upon before proceeding.

The script exports a five-sheet Excel report (`DataCleaning_Report.xlsx`) summarizing each check, a flagged dataset (`SCData_flagged.dta`) containing the original data plus the flag columns, and a processed dataset (`SCData_processed.rds`) that all subsequent analysis scripts load. For this protocol, the processed dataset is identical to the raw data. No flagged observations are dropped, in order to maintain comparability with Xue, Reed, and van Aert (2025). For their own research, researchers should first inspect `DataCleaning_Report.xlsx` and decide which flagged observations should be dropped or revised. They should then apply those changes to the flagged dataset and save the resulting file as `SCData_processed.rds` before running any subsequent scripts. Researchers are also encouraged to maintain a log documenting each change and the reason for it.

**Note for readers using non-Stata data.** The cleaning script reads the raw dataset using `read_dta()` from the `haven` package, which is specific to Stata `.dta` files. If your data are stored in a different format, replace that line with the appropriate R function: `read.csv()` for CSV files, `read_excel()` from `readxl` for Excel files, or `load()` / `readRDS()` for R-native formats. All subsequent scripts load `SCData_processed.rds` using `readRDS()` and require no modification for non-Stata data.

## Run the cleaning script

```{r}
#| label: data-cleaning

source("Protocol_DataCleaning.R")
```

## Inspect the output

```{r}
#| label: data-cleaning-report
#| eval: true

library(readxl)

# View a summary of each quality check
read_excel("DataCleaning_Report.xlsx", sheet = 1)
```

**What to look for.** The researcher should examine whether any observations are flagged by the major standard error check or the coding conflict check, as these are the most likely to reflect genuine errors. Minor standard error discrepancies and small degrees of freedom flags are often a normal feature of the literature and may not require action. True duplicates, if present, should always be investigated. The outlier flags identify extreme effect sizes that may warrant examination in the outlier analysis ([Appendix B](#sec-app-outliers)), but they do not automatically indicate erroneous data.

**Decision point.** For each flagged observation, decide whether to correct it, drop it, or keep it as it is, and record the decision and the reason in the log.

**In this example.** No observations are excluded following this review. The processed dataset is identical to the raw data, and all 957 effect sizes proceed to analysis.

# Preliminary Analysis {#sec-prelim}

Before estimating any formal meta-analytic model, it is useful to characterize the dataset: what variables are available and how the effect sizes are distributed. These two steps correspond to @tbl-table1, @tbl-table2, and @fig-figure1 of the protocol.

## Variable Descriptions {#sec-prelim-vars}

@tbl-table1 provides a reference guide to all variables in the dataset. For continuous variables, it reports the mean, minimum, and maximum. For binary variables, it reports the mean (which equals the proportion of ones) and the number of studies contributing at least one observation with a value of one. The latter is reported to flag cases where a variable takes the value one for many observations but those observations come from only a small number of studies, which can make meta-regression estimates for that variable unreliable. Reference categories are marked with an asterisk.

This table serves two purposes. First, it allows the reader to verify that the dataset matches expectations and that no variables have unexpected ranges or implausible values. Second, it provides the descriptive information needed to interpret the meta-regression coefficients in @sec-metareg, where understanding what each variable represents and what value of one means is essential for forming best-practice predictions.

### Run the script

```{r}
#| label: table1-run

source("Protocol_Variables.R")
```

### Display the output

```{r}
#| label: tbl-table1
#| eval: true
#| tbl-cap: "Variable descriptions."

library(readxl)
library(knitr)

tbl1 <- read_excel("Table_Variables.xlsx")

# The footnote is stored as its own row in the sheet (in the Group column),
# with a blank spacer row above it. Extract the note text, then drop both
# non-data rows, matching the convention used for the other table notes in
# this document.
note_text1 <- tbl1$Group[grepl("^Note:", tbl1$Group)]
tbl1 <- tbl1[!is.na(tbl1$Group) & !grepl("^Note:", tbl1$Group), ]

tbl1 |> knitr::kable()

knitr::asis_output(paste0(
  '<div style="margin-top: 0.25em; text-align: left;"><p><em>', note_text1, '</em></p></div>\n\n'
))
```

**What to look for.** Verify that the effect size variable (`z`) and its standard error (`sez`) have plausible ranges: Fisher's z values for partial correlations are typically bounded between roughly -1 and 1, and standard errors should be positive. For the binary control variables, note which categories are underrepresented, as variables with very few observations coded as one may be collinear with others or may be unreliable in the meta-regression. Pay particular attention to the Studies column: if every observation coded as one comes from a single study or a small number of studies, the variable is effectively a dummy for those studies, and its meta-regression coefficient cannot be cleanly separated from other idiosyncratic features of their design or sample.

**In this example.** `CityLevel` takes the value one for 35 observations, all from a single study, so its coefficient in @tbl-pet-mods should be read with that in mind. The same moderator causes most of the failed bootstrap replications in @sec-mr-selection.

---

## Effect Size Descriptives and Distribution {#sec-prelim-dist}

@tbl-table2 reports descriptive statistics for the effect size distribution: the mean, median, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum of the effect size estimates and their t-statistics, along with the distribution of degrees of freedom. @fig-figure1 displays a histogram of the Fisher's z values, annotated with the mean and with vertical reference lines at the Doucouliagos (2011) threshold of $|z| = 0.07$, the boundary between negligible and small effects in the partial correlation literature.

Doucouliagos (2011) proposed benchmarks of 0.07, 0.17, and 0.33 for small, medium, and large partial correlations in economics, derived from the observed distribution of over 22,000 partial correlations. These are different from Cohen's (1988) thresholds of 0.10, 0.30, and 0.50 because the latter were developed for zero-order (simple) correlations. Applying Cohen's thresholds to partial correlations would systematically understate practical significance, since partial correlations are mechanically smaller once other variables have been partialled out. 

Doucouliagos (2011) was never formally published and is not readily available online, but it remains the standard benchmark for partial correlations in the applied economics meta-analysis literature, with over 150 citing papers recorded on RePEc/IDEAS. Only the small-effect threshold (0.07) is drawn on @fig-figure1. Researchers working with other effect size metrics should replace the Doucouliagos (2011) benchmarks with thresholds appropriate to their context. These values can be substituted directly into the figure script.

An inset table in the figure shows the breakdown of observations by the statistical significance of the associated t-statistic.

These two outputs together give an initial picture of where the evidence is concentrated in the effect size distribution and how much of the literature reports statistically significant results. Both are directly relevant to the publication bias analysis in @sec-pubbias.

### Run the script

```{r}
#| label: table2-figure1-run

source("Protocol_EffectSizes.R")
```

### Display the output

```{r}
#| label: tbl-table2
#| eval: true
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive statistics for the effect size distribution."

read_excel("Table_EffectSizes.xlsx") |> knitr::kable()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-figure1
#| eval: true
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of Fisher's z-transformed effect sizes."

library(knitr)

include_graphics("Figure_EffectSizes.png")
```

**What to look for.** The mean and median effect sizes provide an initial (unadjusted) sense of the central tendency of the literature. A large share of statistically significant results, visible in the inset table, raises the possibility of selective reporting and motivates the formal tests in @sec-pubbias. A distribution that is noticeably skewed or multimodal may suggest that the literature is not homogeneous and that moderator analysis is warranted. The converse does not hold, however: a unimodal, symmetric distribution does not rule out moderator effects, which may be present even when the marginal distribution of effect sizes appears well behaved.

**In this example.** The mean Fisher's z is 0.169 and the median 0.133, which correspond to partial correlations of 0.157 and 0.133. By the Doucouliagos (2011) benchmarks, both lie between a small (0.07) and a medium (0.17) effect. The inset shows that 45.9 percent of the estimates have t-statistics above 2, against only 5.2 percent below -2. That asymmetry is consistent with selective reporting, but not proof of it, since a positive true effect would also produce more significant positive estimates than negative ones. @sec-pubbias examines it formally.

# The Starting Point: Five Models {#sec-estimators}

Before correcting for publication bias, the researcher needs an estimate of the mean effect that allows for the dependence among estimates from the same study. This section builds that estimate in steps. It starts with the two models most often used in practice, fixed effects (FE) and random effects (RE), which treat every estimate as independent. It then adds the two sources of dependence one at a time. The hierarchical effects (HE) model allows estimates from the same study to share part of their true effect. The correlated effects (CE) model allows their sampling errors to be correlated. The correlated and hierarchical effects (CHE) model allows for both. Seeing the five models side by side shows how each source of dependence changes the estimate and its standard error. The CHE estimate is the uncorrected mean effect from which the corrections in @sec-pubbias start.

## The Five Models {#sec-estimators-models}

The five models build on one another. FE and RE ignore the dependence among estimates from the same study. HE and CE each add one source of dependence, and CHE combines both. All are estimated using the `rma.mv()` function from the `metafor` package (Viechtbauer, 2010), with cluster-robust (CR2) standard errors from `clubSandwich` (Pustejovsky, 2026). The five models differ in how they specify the random-effects structure and the variance-covariance matrix of the effect sizes.

**Fixed effects (FE).** No random effects. Each effect size is weighted by the inverse of its known sampling variance. This estimator assumes that the true effect is identical across all studies and all effect sizes, and is included primarily as a baseline for likelihood ratio testing.

**Random effects (RE).** A single observation-level random effect, implemented as `~ 1 | obs` on the individual effect size identifier, so that each effect size estimate receives its own random effect. This is the conventional meta-analytic model and assumes that within-study estimates are conditionally independent.

**Hierarchical effects (HE).** Two random effects, `~ 1 | newid/obs`, with a diagonal variance matrix. This model allows for both between-study and within-study heterogeneity in the true effect, but does not model correlated sampling errors.

**Correlated effects (CE).** A single study-level random effect, implemented as `~ 1 | newid`, combined with an imputed block-diagonal covariance matrix that allows for a constant within-study sampling correlation (denoted $\rho$). This model captures correlated sampling errors but does not allow for within-study heterogeneity in the true effect. In other words, it assumes a common true effect across all estimates within a study, with deviations attributable solely to correlated sampling errors arising from shared samples, correlated outcome measures, and similar sources.

**Correlated and hierarchical effects (CHE).** Two random effects, `~ 1 | newid/obs`, combined with an imputed block-diagonal covariance matrix. This model accommodates between-study heterogeneity, within-study heterogeneity, and correlated sampling errors simultaneously, and is the preferred default model following Pustejovsky and Tipton (2022).

For the CE and CHE models, the imputed block-diagonal covariance matrix is constructed using `vcalc()` from `metafor`, under the assumption of a constant within-study sampling correlation $\rho$. @sec-rho explains how to choose its value.

All five models estimate the mean effect as a weighted average of the individual estimates, but they differ in how they interpret the information from additional estimates. FE and RE treat every estimate as an independent piece of information. Other things equal, a study with 20 estimates therefore counts about 20 times as much as a study with one. In contrast, HE, CE, and CHE recognize that estimates from the same study share that study's true effect, and often its data, so additional estimates tell us more about that one study, but little more about the average across studies. Each additional estimate therefore adds less weight than the one before, and beyond some point a study gains almost nothing by reporting more.

This matters because there are two averages a researcher might want to estimate: the average effect across individual estimates, and the average effect across studies. When effect sizes are unrelated to the number of estimates a study reports, the two averages take the same value, and all five models estimate the same mean. However, when the size of the effect is related to the number of estimates a study reports, the two averages differ. FE and RE give more weight to studies that report many estimates, which pulls their means toward the average across estimates, while HE, CE, and CHE give means closer to the average across studies than FE and RE do. Because the weights also depend on the precision of the estimates, the estimated means need not equal either simple average.

The choice of model therefore also reflects the mean the researcher wants to estimate. In FE and RE, the mean is the average across estimates. In HE, CE, and CHE, it is the average across studies. When the estimates from a study are mostly alternative specifications of the same analysis, as in this example, the average across studies is usually the more natural target.

**More than one level of nesting.** The five models assume a single level of nesting: estimates within studies. Some meta-analyses have a further level, such as several experiments or samples within a paper, each contributing several estimates. CHE extends to this case by adding a random effect for the intermediate level (in `metafor`, `random = ~ 1 | study/sample/estimate`) and by building the sampling covariance matrix within samples rather than within studies (`cluster = sample` in `vcalc()`), since estimates from different samples share no data. Cluster-robust inference is still clustered at the highest level, the study.

## Study Weights and Heterogeneity {#sec-prelim-weights}

@tbl-table3 examines how study weights are distributed across the literature under fixed-effects (FE), random-effects (RE), and hierarchical effects (HE) estimation. Because the dataset contains multiple effect sizes per study, the script first aggregates to the study level by computing a precision-weighted mean effect size for each of the 83 studies, and then fits FE and RE models to the 83 study-level values. Because they are fitted to study-level means, these FE and RE results differ slightly from those in @tbl-table4, which fits the models to all 957 estimates. The HE weights are computed differently: they come from the full observation-level multilevel model, using the row sums of its GLS weight matrix summed to the study level. Under FE, a study's weight is the sum of the precisions of its estimates, so it rises in proportion to the number of estimates the study reports. Under RE fitted to the study means, and under HE, a study gains less weight from each additional estimate, for the reason given in @sec-estimators-models.

The table reports summary statistics of the weight distribution (mean, median, selected percentiles) and the shares of total weight captured by the three and ten largest contributors. It also reports the standard deviation of the true effects between studies, $\hat{\tau}_{\text{study}}$ (RE and HE), and within studies, $\hat{\tau}_{\text{estimate}}$ (HE only), together with $I^2$. Because the RE model here is fitted to the study means, its heterogeneity is between studies. The RE model in @tbl-table4, fitted to all 957 estimates, instead reports the total heterogeneity across estimates.

### Run the script

```{r}
#| label: table3-run

source("Protocol_StudyWeights.R")
```

### Display the output

```{r}
#| label: tbl-table3
#| eval: true
#| tbl-cap: "Study weights and heterogeneity."

readxl::read_excel("Table_StudyWeights.xlsx") |> knitr::kable()
```

**What to look for.** Under FE weighting, weight is concentrated in the most precise (typically largest) studies; under RE weighting, weights are more equalized because the between-study variance places a ceiling on how much any single study can contribute. HE weighting behaves like RE in this respect, since its variance components likewise cap the contribution of any single study. If the weight distribution is highly unequal, for example if the three largest studies account for most of the total FE weight, the overall FE estimate is driven by a small number of studies. This is problematic if the true effects underlying those studies are not representative of the literature as a whole. Judge heterogeneity by $\hat{\tau}_{\text{study}}$ and $\hat{\tau}_{\text{estimate}}$. They are on the same scale as the effect sizes, so they can be compared with the mean effect or with a benchmark for a small effect. $I^2$ is reported because it is widely used, but it does not measure how much the true effects vary (Borenstein et al., 2017). It is the share of the observed variation that is not due to sampling error, so it depends on how precise the estimates are. When the estimates are very precise, $I^2$ is high even if the true effects vary little; when they are imprecise, $I^2$ can be low even if the true effects vary a great deal.

**In this example.** Under FE weighting, the weights are extremely concentrated: one study receives 36.4 percent of the total weight, the three largest 63.3 percent, and the ten largest 89.1 percent. Under RE and HE weighting, the three largest studies receive only 4.0 and 4.6 percent. Heterogeneity is large. Under HE, the standard deviation of the true effects is 0.154 between studies and 0.147 within studies, each comparable in size to the mean effects in @tbl-table4. The case for random effects is clear. $I^2$ is 99.7 percent under RE and 97.8 percent under HE, but these values partly reflect how precise many of the estimates are. The concentration of FE weight is also why @sec-petpeese carries forward CHE-PET-PEESE rather than the CHE-ISCW version, whose weights resemble FE weights.

@tbl-table3 does not report weights for CE and CHE. Both models require an assumed value for the correlation between the sampling errors of estimates from the same study, which the next subsection explains.

## The Choice of Rho {#sec-rho}

Before the five models can be estimated, the researcher must choose a value for $\rho$, the assumed within-study sampling correlation used to construct the imputed block-diagonal covariance matrix for the CE and CHE models. This value governs the degree to which effect size estimates from the same study are treated as correlated in their sampling errors.

This correlation has a true value. It can sometimes be computed from information in the original studies, for example from sample sizes and the degree of sample overlap among estimates (Bom and Rachinger, 2020). Otherwise, it cannot be identified from the effect sizes and standard errors alone, and it cannot be selected by the likelihood or by any other model-comparison criterion. $\rho$ enters the assumed sampling-covariance matrix rather than the random-effects model, so different values of $\rho$ correspond to different assumed data rather than to competing models fit to the same data.

In reality, each pair of estimates probably has its own true correlation, and primary studies rarely report them. The standard practice is therefore to assume a single value for all pairs, commonly $\rho = 0.5$, and to verify by sensitivity analysis that the substantive conclusions do not depend on the value chosen. The simplification matters less than it might appear, because the protocol uses cluster-robust standard errors. A wrong value of $\rho$ affects how efficiently the models use the data, but not the validity of the standard errors and tests, provided the number of studies is not too small (Pustejovsky and Tipton, 2022). When the estimates within a study are alternative specifications estimated on the same data, the true correlation may be well above 0.5, so the sensitivity analysis should extend to high values; the one in [Appendix A](#sec-app-rho) runs to 0.95.

**Decision point.** Adopt a plausible constant value for $\rho$ ($\rho = 0.5$ by default) and, before estimating the five models, run the sensitivity analysis in [Appendix A](#sec-app-rho) to confirm that the substantive conclusions do not depend on the value chosen. Report the value used together with the sensitivity analysis.

**In this example.** The protocol adopts $\rho = 0.5$ throughout. The sensitivity analysis in [Appendix A](#sec-app-rho) shows that the mean effect is stable across the full range of $\rho$.

## Estimation strategy {#sec-estimators-strategy}

All models are estimated using `rma.mv()` from `metafor`. REML is used for the main reported results (the intercept and variance components). ML estimation is used only for the purpose of computing likelihood ratio statistics, since likelihood ratio tests require that both nested models be estimated by the same method (ML rather than REML). Cluster-robust standard errors of the CR2 type (Tipton and Pustejovsky, 2015) are computed using `coef_test()` from `clubSandwich`, with clustering at the study level (`newid`).

The CR2 standard errors are used for all inference throughout this protocol. They are preferable to the model-based standard errors produced by `rma.mv()` because they remain valid even when the working model for the dependence structure is misspecified. Given the complexity of real meta-analytic data, misspecification should be considered the norm rather than the exception (Pustejovsky and Tipton, 2022).

## Choosing the Working Model {#sec-estimators-lr}

The working model should be the simplest one that matches how the data were generated. With cluster-robust standard errors, this choice affects the precision of the estimates, not the validity of the standard errors and tests, provided the number of studies is not too small (Pustejovsky and Tipton, 2022). CHE is the recommended default for most meta-analytic applications because, when studies report several estimates from the same or overlapping samples, it is the simplest of the five models that allows for both sources of dependence: similar true effects within a study, and correlated sampling errors among estimates computed from the same data (Pustejovsky and Tipton, 2022). A simpler model is enough when only one source is present. If the estimates within a study come from independent samples, their sampling errors are uncorrelated, and HE is sufficient. If they measure a single effect with little reason for their true effects to differ, CE is sufficient. When the estimates from a study are different specifications estimated on the same or overlapping samples, as is common in economics, both sources are present and CHE is the natural choice.

@tbl-table4 also reports three likelihood ratio tests (the note below the table gives the comparison each one makes). A significant result indicates that the added variance component is present in the data: between-study heterogeneity for RE against FE, within-study heterogeneity for HE against RE, and within-study heterogeneity in the presence of correlated sampling errors for CHE against CE. A direct test of CHE against HE is not available, because the two models use different sampling covariance matrices. The tests describe the data, but they should not be used to choose the model, for two reasons. First, like the older practice of using the Q-test to choose between fixed and random effects, they can show that a component is needed, but a non-significant result does not show that it can be dropped, because the tests may lack power. Second, the tests are valid only if the working model is correct, including the assumed value of $\rho$. The cluster-robust standard errors used for all other inference in this protocol remain valid even when the working model is wrong, and that is the reason for using them.

## Run the script

```{r}
#| label: table4-run

# Note: this script takes approximately 2 minutes to run.
source("Protocol_FiveEstimators.R")
```

## Display the output

@tbl-table4 presents the five models side by side in a single table, allowing direct comparison of the intercept (the overall mean effect), the standard error, the assumed within-study correlation ($\rho$), the prediction interval, the heterogeneity estimates, and likelihood ratio tests.

The "rho (assumed)" row is shown only for CE and CHE, since these are the two models that use the imputed covariance matrix built with $\rho = 0.5$ (@sec-rho). It is reported as a fixed, assumed value rather than as an estimate: unlike the three tau rows, which the model estimates from the data, $\rho$ is set by the researcher beforehand and used to construct the working covariance matrix. FE, RE, and HE do not use this covariance matrix, so $\rho$ does not apply to them.

The three tau rows report standard deviations of the true effects. The "tau (study)" row is the variation between studies, and the "tau (estimate)" row is the variation among estimates from the same study. The "tau (total)" row combines the two, $\hat{\tau}_{\text{total}}$ $= \sqrt{\hat{\tau}^2_{\text{study}} + \hat{\tau}^2_{\text{estimate}}}$. RE has one random effect for each estimate and ignores which study the estimate comes from, so its single variance component appears only in the \"tau (total)\" row. CE has one random effect for each study, so its \"tau (study)\" and \"tau (total)\" rows are the same. The \"tau (total)\" row is comparable with the total heterogeneity that RoBMA reports in @sec-robma.

The "95% PI" row is the 95% prediction interval. It adds the total heterogeneity to the uncertainty about the mean, so it describes the range within which the true effect underlying a new estimate is expected to fall. As in @sec-mr-petpeese, it does not include sampling error. FE assumes that all estimates share one true effect, so it has no prediction interval.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-table4
#| eval: true
#| tbl-cap: "The five models."

read_excel("Table_FiveEstimators.xlsx", col_types = "text") |> knitr::kable()

knitr::asis_output(paste0(
  '<div style="margin-top: 0.25em; text-align: left;"><p><em>Note: 95% PI = prediction interval for the true effect underlying a new estimate; it does not include sampling error. ',
  'tau (study), tau (estimate), and tau (total) are the standard deviations of the true effects between studies, within studies, and in total. ',
  'The LR test row reports ',
  'the p-value from a likelihood ratio test of that column\'s model against a simpler nested ',
  'alternative, with both models refit via ML for comparability: RE tests RE vs. FE (whether a ',
  'random effect improves fit over no random effects at all); HE tests HE vs. RE (whether a ',
  'second, within-study variance component improves fit); CHE tests CHE vs. CE (whether that ',
  'same within-study variance component improves fit once within-study correlation is already ',
  'modeled). A p-value below the conventional 0.05 threshold favors the more complex (column) ',
  'model over its simpler comparison. FE and CE show no entry because each serves as the ',
  'simpler baseline in one of these comparisons rather than the model being tested; see the ',
  'discussion above for why no direct test of CHE against HE is available.</em></p></div>\n\n'
))
```

**What to look for.** The primary quantity of interest is the CHE intercept, which gives the overall mean effect after accounting for both between-study and within-study heterogeneity and for correlated sampling errors. $\hat{\tau}_{\text{study}}$ and $\hat{\tau}_{\text{estimate}}$ divide the total heterogeneity into its between-study and within-study parts. When $\hat{\tau}_{\text{estimate}}$ is large relative to $\hat{\tau}_{\text{study}}$, moderator variables that vary within studies (such as the type of outcome measure) are likely to be more informative than those that vary only between studies. Then compare the confidence interval with the prediction interval. The confidence interval shows how precisely the mean is estimated; the prediction interval shows how widely the true effects are spread around it. A narrow confidence interval with a wide prediction interval means that the mean is well estimated, but that the true effects in the literature differ substantially.

**Decision point.** Choose the working model for all subsequent analysis. This protocol recommends CHE on a priori grounds: it is the only one of the five models that allows for both sources of dependence. Choosing CHE also means that the target is the average across studies (@sec-estimators-models). If the research question instead concerns the average across estimates, FE or RE is the more appropriate model. The likelihood ratio tests in @tbl-table4 describe the data, but they should not decide the choice (@sec-estimators-lr).

**In this example.** CHE is selected for all subsequent analysis because the estimates within each study are alternative specifications estimated on the same data, so both sources of dependence are present. The likelihood ratio tests are consistent with this choice: each added variance component is significant (p < 0.0001 in all three tests). The two variance components are similar in magnitude ($\hat{\tau}_{\text{study}}$ = 0.127 and $\hat{\tau}_{\text{estimate}}$ = 0.157), so heterogeneity is divided roughly equally between and within studies. The uncorrected CHE mean is 0.175, with a 95% confidence interval of [0.139, 0.212]. Its 95% prediction interval is [-0.229, 0.579]. By the Doucouliagos (2011) benchmarks, it runs from a negative effect beyond the medium-effect threshold to a large positive effect. The mean is well estimated, but the true effects in this literature differ substantially.

The estimates illustrate the points made in @sec-estimators-models. The simple average across all 957 estimates is 0.169, and the simple average across the 83 studies is 0.229. The two differ because effect sizes are related to the number of estimates a study reports. The 23 studies that report one to three estimates have an average effect of 0.367, compared with 0.158 for the 30 studies that report 11 or more. RE gives a mean of 0.145 and FE a mean of 0.063, both below the two simple averages, because the most precise estimates in this literature report the smallest effects. HE, CE, and CHE give means between 0.175 and 0.194. These are closer to the average across studies than the FE and RE means, but still nearer the average across estimates.

---

# Publication Bias: Three Corrections {#sec-pubbias}

A persistent concern in any meta-analysis is selective reporting: the possibility that the available effect size estimates are not a representative sample of all the estimates researchers produced on the topic. Selection can occur at two levels. Whole studies may go unpublished, and within a study, researchers may choose which of several specifications to report. In either case, the estimates most likely to be reported are those that are statistically significant, those that have the expected sign, or both. When selective reporting is present, meta-analytic estimates are biased in the direction of the expected sign, because the literature over-represents estimates that are significant and of the expected sign.

@sec-estimators estimated the mean effect without allowing for selective reporting. This section asks two further questions. Is there evidence of selective reporting? And if so, how much does correcting for it change the estimate? Each correction supplies its own evidence on the first question: the FAT slope of the PET regression, the selection weights of the step-function models, and RoBMA's inclusion Bayes factor for publication bias. The protocol does not, however, use a significance test to decide whether to correct. Tests for publication bias can have low power, particularly when a meta-analysis includes few studies (Macaskill, Walter, and Irwig, 2001; Furuya-Kanamori et al., 2020). In any case, a failure to detect bias is not evidence that none exists. Instead, the corrected estimates are reported alongside the uncorrected estimates in @tbl-table4. RoBMA treats the question differently. Because it averages over models with and without publication bias, it needs no pretest: if the data give little support to selective reporting, the bias models receive little weight and its estimate moves toward the uncorrected one.

Three approaches to correcting for selective reporting are in current use, and this protocol applies all three. They address the same question, but they make different assumptions about how selection operates. @tbl-approaches summarizes them.

| Approach | What it assumes about selection | What it reports |
|:---|:---|:---|
| CHE-PET-PEESE (regression-based) | Selection is approximated by the association between effect size and standard error; larger, more precise studies are assumed to be less affected. | A bias-adjusted mean, extrapolated to a study of perfect precision, plus a test for small-study effects. |
| Step-function selection models (3PSM and 4PSM) | The probability that an estimate is reported changes at fixed one-sided p-value thresholds: 0.025 (significance) in both models, and also 0.5 (sign) in 4PSM. | A corrected mean, plus the estimated relative probability that estimates in each p-value interval are reported. |
| RoBMA (model-averaged) | Does not commit to one model of selection. Averages over models with and without an effect, heterogeneity, and publication bias, where the bias models include six step functions together with PET and PEESE. | A model-averaged corrected mean, inclusion Bayes factors for each component, and the estimated selection weights. |

: Three approaches to publication-bias correction. {#tbl-approaches}

The section proceeds in four steps, starting with the methods readers are most likely to know: the funnel plot and Egger-type regressions are by far the most common tools for assessing publication bias (Wu, Duan, Reed, and Tipton, 2026). @sec-funnel presents the funnel plot, a visual first look. Sections [-@sec-petpeese] to [-@sec-robma] then estimate each of the three corrections before any moderators are added. Here and below, moderators are the variables listed in @tbl-table1 that describe the data, samples, and estimation procedures behind each estimate. For PET-PEESE, the regression at this stage contains an intercept plus a bias term (the standard error or its square); the bias term is part of the correction, not a moderator. Estimating all three under the same conditions makes their results directly comparable. @sec-diagnosis uses these results, together with two diagnostics, to choose one correction as the primary method. @sec-metareg returns to all three corrections and adds the study characteristics as moderators.

Wherever possible, the corrections use the dependence model chosen in @sec-estimators. PET-PEESE and RoBMA both use CHE to model the dependence among estimates. The selection models are the exception. Their estimates come from a random-effects-type model that treats the estimates as independent. Dependence enters only through inference: confidence intervals are calculated from a cluster bootstrap (see @sec-selection).

## Funnel Plot {#sec-funnel}

The funnel plot is a scatterplot of effect sizes against their standard errors. In the absence of selective reporting, it should be approximately symmetric around the pooled estimate: small studies with large standard errors scatter widely around the center, while large studies cluster tightly near the pooled effect. Asymmetry, in particular a tendency for small studies to cluster on the side of larger effects, is a visual signal of small-study effects, which may reflect selective reporting.

The funnel plot is constructed using a univariate RE model estimated by `rma()` rather than `rma.mv()`. This is conventional: the funnel plot is a descriptive tool and does not depend on the full multivariate dependence structure. Its purpose is purely visual and motivational.

### Run the script

```{r}
#| label: figure2-run

source("Protocol_FunnelPlot.R")
```

### Display the output

```{r}
#| label: fig-figure2
#| eval: true
#| fig-cap: "Funnel plot of effect sizes against standard errors."

knitr::include_graphics("Figure_FunnelPlot.png")
```

**What to look for.** Pronounced asymmetry, where the lower portion of the funnel (small studies) is denser on the positive side, is consistent with selective reporting of positive results. However, funnel plot asymmetry can also arise from genuine heterogeneity, methodological differences correlated with study size, or other sources unrelated to publication bias. The funnel plot should therefore be treated as suggestive rather than conclusive. Nor does a funnel plot that looks symmetric show that publication bias is absent: only strong selection is likely to be visible by eye (Terrin, Schmid, and Lau, 2005). Its visual message is tested formally in the sections that follow.

**In this example.** The funnel is clearly asymmetric. The most precise estimates cluster just above zero, while less precise estimates lie increasingly to the right. The lower left of the funnel, where imprecise negative estimates would appear, is sparsely populated. This is the pattern selective reporting would produce, and the corrections below test it formally.

---

## CHE-PET-PEESE {#sec-petpeese}

The funnel asymmetry test (FAT) and precision-effect test (PET), due to Egger et al. (1997) and Stanley and Doucouliagos (2014) respectively, translate the visual inspection of the funnel plot into a formal regression framework. Before moderators are added, the FAT-PET regression contains an intercept plus a bias term:

$$T_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{SE}_{ij} + u_j + v_{ij} + e_{ij},$$

where $T_{ij}$ is effect size estimate $i$ from study $j$ and $\text{SE}_{ij}$ is its standard error. The slope coefficient $\hat{\beta}_1$ is the FAT test: a significantly positive estimate indicates that larger effects are observed precisely where standard errors are larger, which is consistent with selective reporting of significant results. The intercept $\hat{\beta}_0$ is the PET estimator of the mean effect net of bias. It is the predicted effect size for a hypothetical study with a standard error of zero, that is, a study of infinite precision, which cannot have been selectively reported on the basis of significance.

The precision-effect estimate with standard error (PEESE) replaces $\text{SE}_{ij}$ with its square. Stanley and Doucouliagos (2014) show that PET underestimates the mean effect when a genuine effect is present, and that PEESE's quadratic correction is then more appropriate. The PET-PEESE rule therefore reports PET unless the PET intercept is positive and statistically significant, in which case it reports PEESE. Following Chen and Pustejovsky (2026), this protocol treats the intercept as significant when its two-sided p-value is below 0.10, which is a one-sided test at the 5 percent level.

In the dependent-effects context, both regressions are estimated using `rma.mv()` with the full CHE variance structure and CR2 standard errors, following Rodgers and Pustejovsky (2021) and Chen and Pustejovsky (2026). This extends the conventional Egger regression to the multivariate setting without abandoning the dependence structure.

**Why no moderators yet?** The regression above contains only an intercept and the bias term. This section asks how much correcting for selective reporting changes the mean effect in @tbl-table4, which contains no moderators. Leaving moderators out keeps the two estimates comparable, so their difference reflects the correction alone. @sec-metareg adds moderators to each of the three corrections. Omitting them here comes at a cost. When the standard error is correlated with moderators, this regression can mistake systematic heterogeneity for selective reporting. Wu, Duan, Reed, and Tipton (2026) find that regression-based corrections in practice almost always use this univariate form, and they recommend adding moderators that may be correlated with the standard error. @sec-mr-petpeese does exactly that, and it gives the more informative test. Both scripts below estimate the two versions; this section reports the version without moderators (Panel A).

### Run the scripts

```{r}
#| label: table5-run

# Note: each script takes 5 to 7 minutes to run.
source("Protocol_CHE_PET.R")    # PET
source("Protocol_CHE_PEESE.R")   # PEESE
```

### Display the output

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pet
#| eval: true
#| tbl-cap: "CHE-PET, intercept plus bias term."

read_excel("Table_CHE_PET.xlsx", sheet = 1, col_types = "text") |> knitr::kable()

knitr::asis_output(paste0(
  '<div style="margin-top: 0.25em; text-align: left;"><p><em>Note: "Effect beyond bias" is the PET intercept; ',
  '"Bias" is the coefficient on the standard error (the FAT test). The table reports all five estimators; ',
  'the CHE column is the one carried forward. The LR test row reports ',
  'the p-value from a likelihood ratio test of that column\'s model against a simpler nested ',
  'alternative, with both models refit via ML for comparability: RE tests RE vs. FE; HE tests HE vs. RE; ',
  'CHE tests CHE vs. CE (see Section 4).</em></p></div>\n\n'
))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-peese
#| eval: true
#| tbl-cap: "CHE-PEESE, intercept plus bias term."

read_excel("Table_CHE_PEESE.xlsx", sheet = 1, col_types = "text") |> knitr::kable()
```

**What to look for.** Start with the FAT slope, the "Bias" row in @tbl-pet. Strictly speaking, this is a test for small-study effects rather than for publication bias itself, the same distinction noted for the funnel plot above. A significant slope is consistent with selective reporting, but genuine heterogeneity or other design differences correlated with study precision can produce the same pattern.

As noted at the start of this section, a non-significant FAT slope does not rule out publication bias. The protocol therefore applies the PET correction and reports its intercept regardless of whether the FAT slope is significant.

Then turn to the intercept, the "Effect beyond bias" row. It estimates the mean effect for a study with a standard error of zero. Compare it with the uncorrected CHE mean in @tbl-table4 to see how far the correction moves the estimate, and check whether its confidence interval includes zero.

**Decision point.** Apply the PET-PEESE rule. Use the CHE-PET intercept as the corrected mean effect unless it is positive and statistically significant (two-sided p < 0.10), in which case use the CHE-PEESE intercept in @tbl-peese. Report @tbl-peese in either case, for transparency.

**In this example.** The CHE FAT slope is large and highly significant (1.575, SE = 0.252). The CHE-PET intercept is 0.028, with a 95% confidence interval of [-0.014, 0.070]. That is a reduction of 84 percent from the uncorrected CHE mean of 0.175 (@tbl-table4), and the interval includes zero. Because the CHE-PET intercept is not statistically significant, PET is retained as the PET-PEESE estimate. The CHE-PEESE intercept of 0.102 in @tbl-peese is reported for transparency only.

### Robustness check: CHE-ISCW-PET-PEESE

CHE-PET-PEESE uses the conventional CHE weights: each estimate is weighted by the inverse of its total variance, which includes both sampling error and the CHE random effects. Chen and Pustejovsky (2026) propose an alternative, inverse sampling covariance weights (ISCW). The weight matrix for each study is set to $\mathbf{W}_j = \mathbf{S}_j^{-1}$, where $\mathbf{S}_j$ is the sampling variance-covariance matrix of the effect sizes in study $j$ (constructed under the assumed $\rho$). These weights give relatively more weight to large studies, which have smaller sampling variances and are less susceptible to selective reporting. Chen and Pustejovsky use ISCW weights for their own version of PET-PEESE.

The robustness check, CHE-ISCW-PET-PEESE, re-estimates CHE-PET-PEESE with ISCW weights. It uses the bias term that the PET-PEESE rule selected for the main estimate (the standard error for PET, its square for PEESE), so the two estimates differ only in their weights. @tbl-iscw places the main CHE-PET-PEESE estimate (repeated from @tbl-pet) next to its ISCW version. It also reports the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom for each mean effect. These indicate how many studies effectively inform the estimate: when a few studies carry most of the weight, as can happen with ISCW weights, the degrees of freedom are small and the CR2 confidence interval becomes unreliable.

```{r}
#| label: iscw-run

# Note: this script takes two to three minutes to run. It estimates both
# columns.
source("Protocol_CHE_ISCW.R")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-iscw
#| eval: true
#| tbl-cap: "Robustness check on the weights used by CHE-PET-PEESE."

tbl_iscw <- read_excel("Table_CHE_ISCW.xlsx", sheet = "Display")
# Older output files label the main column "CHE PET-PEESE"; use the hyphenated name
names(tbl_iscw) <- sub("^CHE PET-PEESE$", "CHE-PET-PEESE", names(tbl_iscw))
tbl_iscw |> knitr::kable(align = "lrr")
```

**What to look for.** Compare the two columns. Because they differ only in their weights, the question is whether giving the most precise estimates more weight changes the result once the bias term is included. Similar intercepts and bias coefficients mean that the PET-PEESE estimate is robust to the weighting scheme.

If the values differ substantially, the bias term selected by the PET-PEESE rule may be too simple to capture the relationship between estimated effects and their standard errors. The PET-PEESE intercept is an extrapolation to a standard error of zero. ISCW weights give the most weight to the most precise estimates, which lie closest to that point, so CHE-ISCW-PET-PEESE depends less on getting the shape of the relationship right. In that case it is the more robust of the two estimates, provided the most precise studies are representative.

The table also shows which version to carry forward. ISCW weights are the better choice when studies are fairly evenly sized, because they reduce the influence of the small studies most prone to selective reporting. However, they are a poor choice when a few studies dominate the weights. To check, look at the fixed-effect column of @tbl-table3, which ISCW weights closely resemble, and at the degrees of freedom in the table; Tipton (2015) advises against interpreting robust variance estimates with fewer than 4.

**In this example.** The PET-PEESE rule selects PET, so both columns use the standard error as the bias term. Their intercepts are 0.028 and 0.027, and their bias coefficients are 1.575 and 1.563. Giving the most precise estimates more weight therefore makes almost no difference. Further, the weights are heavily concentrated. Under fixed-effect weighting, the three largest studies account for 63.3 percent of the total weight, compared with 4.0 percent under RE and 4.6 percent under HE weighting (@tbl-table3). As a result, the ISCW estimate rests on only 4.3 degrees of freedom, against 24.6 for CHE-PET-PEESE. The rest of the protocol therefore uses CHE-PET-PEESE, including the meta-regression in @sec-mr-petpeese.

---

## Selection Models {#sec-selection}

PET-PEESE infers selection indirectly, from a small-study effect. Step-function selection models take the opposite approach: they specify how selection operates and estimate it (Hedges and Vevea, 1996). They assume that the probability an estimate is reported depends on which interval its one-sided p-value falls into. Estimates that are significant and of the expected sign serve as the reference category, with a weight of 1. The model estimates the relative probability, $\lambda$, that estimates in each of the other intervals are reported. A value of $\lambda$ close to 1 indicates little selection against that interval; a value well below 1 indicates that such estimates are under-reported. The corrected mean is the mean of the distribution of effects before selection, estimated by reweighting the observed estimates for these differences.

The choice of intervals determines what kind of selection the model can detect. In what follows, the expected sign is taken to be positive, as in this dataset. The three-parameter selection model (3PSM) uses a single threshold at a one-sided p-value of 0.025, which corresponds to two-sided significance at the 5 percent level. It allows significant results to be favored over insignificant ones, but it treats an insignificant estimate of the expected sign and a wrong-signed estimate alike.

The four-parameter selection model (4PSM) adds a second threshold at 0.5, which separates positive from negative estimates. It therefore estimates two weights: $\lambda_1$ for insignificant estimates of the expected sign, and $\lambda_2$ for wrong-signed estimates. The protocol estimates both models. 

Because 4PSM contains 3PSM as a special case (3PSM is 4PSM with $\lambda_2 = \lambda_1$), comparing the two weights shows whether the extra threshold is needed. @sec-diagnosis uses this comparison, together with the z-plot, to decide which selection model to rely on. Both models assume that researchers favor significant results of the expected sign. A literature with no expected sign calls for a different step-function model, with significance thresholds on both sides of zero; RoBMA's set of selection models already includes such two-sided models.

For dependent effect sizes, both models are estimated by penalized marginal likelihood (PML) using the `metaselection` package (Pustejovsky, Citkowicz, and Joshi, 2026). PML treats each estimate as if it were marginally independent and adds a weak penalty that keeps the estimates in a plausible range. Dependence is addressed through the confidence intervals, which come from a two-stage cluster bootstrap: studies are resampled first, and then estimates within studies. 

**A note on comparing the selection models with CHE estimates.** Because the selection models treat estimates as marginally independent, as the RE model does, they weight the estimates as RE does: a study with more estimates counts for more. Their mean is therefore closer to the average effect across estimates (@sec-estimators-models). Dependence therefore affects only their confidence intervals, not their point estimates. This differs from the CHE model, where dependence also affects the point estimates. As a result, differences between the bias-adjusted selection-model and CHE estimates can reflect how the estimates are weighted, rather than only the different ways of handling publication bias. A simple check is to compare the uncorrected RE and CHE means in @tbl-table4: the closer they are, the less the weighting can explain. Here they are 0.145 and 0.175.

**A note on the penalty priors.** The default priors supplied by `define_priors()` are calibrated for standardized effect sizes such as Fisher's $z$. For a nonstandard effect size, such as a raw regression coefficient, the prior on the mean may be poorly suited to the scale of the data and should be adjusted (see Pustejovsky, Citkowicz, and Joshi, 2026).

### Run the script

```{r}
#| label: selection-run

# Loads the saved fits by default (seconds). With refit <- TRUE, it refits
# both models with the bootstrap (R = 1999 each): about 3 minutes with four
# processor cores, longer with fewer.
source("Protocol_SelectionModels.R")
```

### Display the output

```{r}
#| label: tbl-selection
#| eval: true
#| tbl-cap: "Step-function selection models."

tbl_sel <- read_excel("Table_SelectionModels.xlsx", sheet = "Display")
# Shorten the lambda row labels; lambda1 means different things in the two
# models, so the note below defines each weight for each model
tbl_sel$Parameter <- sub("^lambda1:.*", "lambda1", tbl_sel$Parameter)
tbl_sel$Parameter <- sub("^lambda2:.*", "lambda2", tbl_sel$Parameter)
# Report bootstrap intervals only; drop the large-sample SE and CI rows
tbl_sel <- tbl_sel[!tbl_sel$Parameter %in% c("(SE)", "95% CI (large-sample)"), ]
tbl_sel |> knitr::kable(align = "lrr")

knitr::asis_output(paste0(
  '<div style="margin-top: 0.25em; text-align: left;"><p><em>Note: Bootstrap intervals are percentile ',
  'intervals from a two-stage cluster bootstrap with 1,999 replications. ',
  'In 4PSM, lambda1 is the weight for insignificant estimates of the expected sign ',
  '(one-sided p between 0.025 and 0.5), and lambda2 is the weight for wrong-signed estimates ',
  '(one-sided p above 0.5). In 3PSM, lambda1 covers every estimate that is not significant and ',
  'positive, including wrong-signed estimates; 3PSM has no lambda2. The reference category ',
  '(significant at 5 percent, expected sign) has a weight of 1.</em></p></div>\n\n'
))
```

**What to look for.** The two models differ in one respect: whether wrong-signed estimates are treated separately. Start, therefore, with the selection weights. A weight close to 1 means that estimates in that interval are reported about as often as significant estimates of the expected sign; a weight well below 1 means that they are under-reported. Compare the two weights in the 4PSM. If $\hat{\lambda}_2$ is well below $\hat{\lambda}_1$, selection operates on sign, and 3PSM, which forces the two to be equal, will correct too little. Read the intervals with care, since bootstrap intervals for selection weights tend to be too narrow. Then compare the corrected means of the two models. If they differ, the choice between them is a question about the selection process, which @sec-diagnosis takes up.

**In this example.** In 3PSM, the single weight $\hat{\lambda}_1$ for every estimate that is not significant and positive is 0.75, with a bootstrap interval of [0.29, 1.50]. The 4PSM splits this category in two. Its weight for insignificant estimates of the expected sign is 0.79 [0.31, 1.55], an interval that includes 1. Its weight for wrong-signed estimates, $\hat{\lambda}_2$, is 0.27 [0.06, 0.91], an interval that excludes 1. Wrong-signed estimates appear to be reported only about a quarter as often as significant positive ones, and about a third as often as insignificant positive ones. Given the caution about bootstrap intervals, this is suggestive rather than decisive; @sec-diagnosis asks whether RoBMA's selection weights and the z-plot tell the same story.

The corrected means differ accordingly. The 4PSM gives 0.050 [-0.047, 0.129], 71 percent below the uncorrected CHE mean, with an interval that includes zero. 3PSM gives 0.124 [0.057, 0.182]. The difference arises because 3PSM, by combining wrong-signed and insignificant positive estimates, cannot register a shortage of negative estimates specifically. If selection operates on sign, a model that cannot see it corrects too little.

---

## RoBMA {#sec-robma}

PET-PEESE and the selection models each commit to one account of how selection operates. Robust Bayesian Meta-Analysis (RoBMA; Maier, Bartoš, and Wagenmakers, 2023; Bartoš et al., 2023) does not. Instead, it averages over a set of models, weighting each by its posterior probability, and lets the data decide how much weight each account of selection receives. This subsection builds RoBMA in two steps. Step 1 averages over models that differ only in whether they include an effect and heterogeneity, with no allowance for publication bias. Step 2 adds the publication-bias component. Comparing the two steps shows what the correction does.

RoBMA reports two kinds of results. The first is a set of model-averaged estimates of the model's parameters: the mean effect, the heterogeneity, and the parameters of the publication-bias models, such as the selection weights. The second is a set of inclusion Bayes factors. These measure how strongly the data favor models that include a component (an effect, heterogeneity, or publication bias) over models that exclude it. In other words, they ask whether the parameter belongs in the model at all. A Bayes factor above 1 favors including the component, and one below 1 favors excluding it. Following Lee and Wagenmakers (2013), who adapt Jeffreys (1961), values between 1/3 and 3 are weak evidence either way, values above 3 are moderate evidence, values above 10 strong evidence, and values above 100 extreme evidence. These labels are rough guides, not fixed cut-offs. Whether there is an effect is a question for the inclusion Bayes factor, not for whether a credible interval happens to include zero.

Version 4.0 of the `RoBMA` package implements the multilevel model of Bartoš, Maier, and Wagenmakers (2026). It allows for the clustering of estimates within studies but not for correlated sampling errors, so it corresponds to the HE model rather than to CHE. Version 4.1 adds the function `RoBMA.mv()`, which takes the same imputed sampling covariance matrix and the same study-level and estimate-level random effects as the CHE model. All RoBMA results in this protocol use this CHE specification, with $\rho = 0.5$ as in @sec-estimators.

**Software.** `RoBMA.mv()` requires version 4.1.1 or later of the `RoBMA` package, which is available on CRAN together with the version of `BayesTools` it depends on. `Protocol_Install.R` (@sec-software) installs both; the line that does so is shown below. Restart R after installing. RoBMA also requires JAGS (see Software Setup in the Introduction).

```{r}
#| label: robma-install

install.packages(c("BayesTools", "RoBMA"))
```

**What about other effect sizes?** This protocol illustrates RoBMA using Fisher's z-transformed partial correlations (`measure = "ZCOR"`). RoBMA accepts five other standardized effect sizes directly: standardized mean differences (`"SMD"`), risk ratios (`"RR"`), odds ratios (`"OR"`), hazard ratios (`"HR"`), and incidence rate ratios (`"IRR"`). Each has a known unit information standard deviation built into the package, which lets RoBMA scale its default priors automatically. A nonstandard effect size, such as a raw regression coefficient, requires `measure = "GEN"` together with either sample sizes or a manually supplied scaling factor. The procedure is described in a comment at the end of `Protocol_RoBMA_CHE_Intercept.R`.

**A note on MCMC convergence.** Before interpreting output from any RoBMA model, the researcher should confirm that the MCMC chains have converged. RoBMA applies automatic convergence checks to every fitted model, by default requiring an R-hat below 1.05 and an effective sample size (ESS) of at least 500, and prints a warning whenever a model fails them. These warnings should not be ignored. The remedy is to increase the sampling effort (the `sample`, `burnin`, `adapt`, and `thin` settings) or to refit with `autofit = TRUE`, which extends the chains until the criteria are met. The tables below report R-hat and ESS directly, and `plot_diagnostic()` produces trace, autocorrelation, and density plots for individual parameters.

### Run the script

```{r}
#| label: robma-intercept-run

# Loads the saved fits by default (seconds). With refit <- TRUE, it refits
# both models: about 3.5 hours for RoBMA.mv and a few minutes for BMA.mv.
source("Protocol_RoBMA_CHE_Intercept.R")
```

### Step 1: Model averaging without a publication-bias correction

The function `BMA.mv()` fits RoBMA without its publication-bias component. It averages over four models, formed by crossing the presence or absence of an effect with the presence or absence of heterogeneity. All four use the same imputed covariance matrix for the sampling errors.

1. No effect, no heterogeneity: the mean is fixed at zero, and estimates differ only through their correlated sampling errors.
2. Effect, no heterogeneity: a fixed-effect model with correlated sampling errors.
3. No effect, heterogeneity: the CHE model with the mean fixed at zero.
4. Effect, heterogeneity: the CHE model of @sec-estimators, estimated with priors.

Comparing models 2 and 4 with models 1 and 3 tests whether there is an effect, averaging over the uncertainty about heterogeneity. Comparing models 3 and 4 with models 1 and 2 tests whether there is heterogeneity, averaging over the uncertainty about the effect. These two comparisons give the inclusion Bayes factors in Panel A of @tbl-bma-intercept. The effect and heterogeneity components each have a prior probability of 0.5, so each of the four models starts with a prior probability of 0.25. The data then shift this weight toward the models that fit best.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bma-intercept
#| eval: true
#| tbl-cap: "Bayesian model averaging without a publication-bias correction (BMA)."

# The saved tables hold both the BMA.mv() results (Step 1) and the RoBMA.mv()
# results (Step 2). keep_model() keeps one model's columns and drops its prefix.
keep_model <- function(tbl, model) {
  other <- setdiff(c("RoBMA", "BMA"), model)
  tbl <- tbl[, !startsWith(names(tbl), paste0(other, ":")), drop = FALSE]
  names(tbl) <- sub(paste0("^", model, ": (.)"), "\\U\\1", names(tbl), perl = TRUE)
  tbl
}
# Left-align the first column and right-align the rest, however many there are
align_lr <- function(tbl) c("l", rep("r", ncol(tbl) - 1))
# Label the posterior mean explicitly
post_mean <- function(tbl) { names(tbl)[names(tbl) == "Mean"] <- "Posterior mean"; tbl }

bma_a <- read_excel("Table_RoBMA_CHE_Intercept.xlsx", sheet = "Components") |> keep_model("BMA")
bma_a <- bma_a[bma_a$Component != "Publication bias", ]   # BMA has no bias component
knitr::kable(bma_a, align = align_lr(bma_a), caption = "Panel A: Inclusion of model components")
bma_b <- read_excel("Table_RoBMA_CHE_Intercept.xlsx", sheet = "Estimates") |> keep_model("BMA") |> post_mean()
bma_b <- bma_b[bma_b$Parameter != "Mean effect, conditional on an effect", ]
knitr::kable(bma_b, align = align_lr(bma_b), caption = "Panel B: Mean effect and heterogeneity (Fisher's z)")

knitr::asis_output(paste0(
  '<div style="margin-top: 0.25em; text-align: left;"><p><em>Note: ',
  'CrI = credible interval; ESS = effective sample size. ',
  'Bayes factors marked ">" are lower bounds: every posterior draw fell in models that include the component.',
  '</em></p></div>\n\n'
))
```

**What to look for.** Panel A shows whether the data favor including an effect and heterogeneity. A posterior probability well above the prior of 0.5, and an inclusion Bayes factor well above 1, favor including the component. Panel B gives the model-averaged mean. Compare it with the frequentist CHE mean in @tbl-table4. Close agreement means that the models without an effect receive negligible weight, so the averaging reduces to the CHE model, and that the priors within that model have little influence. If the models without an effect receive substantial weight, the model-averaged mean is pulled toward zero.

**In this example.** The data provide extreme evidence both for an effect and for heterogeneity: every posterior draw fell in the CHE model, which includes both. The mean is 0.174 [0.138, 0.214], essentially the frequentist CHE mean of 0.175 [0.139, 0.212]. Total heterogeneity ($\tau_{\text{total}}$) is 0.203, close to the frequentist CHE value of 0.202 in @tbl-table4, with about 40 percent of it between studies.

### Step 2: Adding the publication-bias component

The function `RoBMA.mv()` adds the publication-bias component. This component has nine options: no publication bias, six step-function selection models with different thresholds, PET, and PEESE.
